newsitem.title: RWANDA: U.N. to keep Rwanda operation going after killings.
newsitem.headline: U.N. to keep Rwanda operation going after killings.

text.p: The U.N. refused on Monday to suspend activities in any part of Rwanda after three Spanish aid workers were murdered and an American badly wounded in an attack in a northwestern town at the weekend.
"We are not going to succumb to terrorist activities. The people who did this would only get what they wanted if we tucked up our tails and ran," said U.N. spokesman John McMillan.
But other aid officials privately criticised the decision, saying it could lead to more expatriate deaths.
"There is absolutely no way we are going to start risking the lives of staff for the sake of providing humanitarian services," said a senior aid official.

In the worst deliberate attack against foreigners working in the country, Hutu militiamen of the former Rwandan government shot dead three Spanish aid workers from the Medicos del Mundo (Doctors of the World) agency in an overnight attack in the northwestern town of Ruhengeri on Sunday.
Three Rwandan soldiers were also killed in the attack and an American seriously wounded and later evacuated.

The killers were said by Rwandan military sources to have belonged to the Hutu Interahamwe militia that played a leading role in the 1994 slaughter of 800,000 Rwandans, mostly minority Tutsis, before being driven into Zaire by Tutsi rebels.
The European Union expressed shock on Monday over the killing, saying the incident underlined the need for international mediation in the region.
"The events during the weekend underline the continuing need for a global solution to the problems of the region," EU foreign ministers said in a statement.

In a press release issued in the Rwandan capital the U.N. said heads of agencies and non-governmental organisations had met the defence ministry to discuss security. One option was thought to be suspension of activities in the north west.
One group has already suspended operations in the small Central African country and Spain has advised its nationals to leave.
Aid officials shocked by the killings were bitterly critical of the U.N. stance over the latest in a series of attacks singling out Omar Bahket, U.N. Rwanda Coordinator for criticism.
"What does he want, more expatriate corpses? He should spend time thinking about this, rather than trying to impress the Rwandan government," said an aid official speaking on condition of anonymity.

"The problem is that with the five attacks of the last 10 days in which aid agencies are being deliberately targeted, there is a dangerous threat and it is not being taken seriously," another senior aid official said.
Earlier the U.N. said aid operations in Ruhengeri would be limited to the daytime and expatriate workers would not be allowed to spend a night in the city, which is close to Zaire's border.
Former militiamen are believed to have infiltrated Rwanda among the mass of over 500,000 refugees who returned to their homeland from Zaire late last year.
Medicos del Mundo named the dead as Dr Manuel Madrazo, 42, nurse Maria Flors Sirera, 33, and Luis Valtuena, 30. The American was Nitin Madhav, 28, from the Pittsburgh area of Pennyslvania.

In Paris, the parent group Medecins du Monde announced that it was suspending all activities in Rwanda pending further information about the killings. Most expatriates in the Ruhengeri area have left for Kigali.
